# Intergenerational knowledge exchange: separating age, career stage, and cohort labels

Narrative review draft (v2, full-text appraised) · not submission-ready · 9 October 2026

## Review question

What can research establish about knowledge exchange across career stages without treating generation labels as causal explanations?

Focus confirmed by the author on 9 October 2026 ([decisions](question-decisions.md)).

## Evidence base and method

The author's folder (`Paper 15 Oct 2024/References`) holds 21 PDFs. All were identified against Crossref, and none is retracted. Six were excluded because "generation" meant something else, such as family-firm succession, migrant generation or parent-child income, or because no work comparison was made (`screening.json`). Fifteen were included and coded for design logic (`coding.json`):

- **GENCAT**: generation category entered as a predictor or moderator (10 studies)
- **XSEC**: a single cross-section, where age, career stage, period and cohort are confounded (6)
- **COHORT**: a design able to separate cohort from age, such as replicated cross-sections or time-lag samples (3)
- **WITHIN**: tests of heterogeneity inside one generation (1)
- **KT**: knowledge or skill transmission across generations (3)

Quotes were checked against the cited PDF pages.

## What the collection shows

### 1. Most comparisons cannot attribute differences to generation

Six included studies compare generation groups measured at one point in time [R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6]. In such data a "Millennial vs. Gen X" difference is equally a difference in age, career stage and tenure. Several of these studies nonetheless frame results as generational. They report, for example, that relationships held "for millennials" but not "for older employees" [R5, PDF p8], or that "generational diversity" moderates job crafting and boredom [R6, abstract]. Results are also mixed: in Canadian public servants, "Generational cohort had little impact on the importance of work values" [R2, abstract].

### 2. Designs that can separate cohort from age find small or specific differences

Three included studies use designs that hold age constant across time:

- **Time-lag with constant age bands.** Two independent samples of the urban Turkish workforce (1998 and 2009, N = 779) let the authors "cross-temporally analyze generational change and rule out the confounding effects of age and career effects on culturally related personal values" [R7, PDF p2]. They found decreases in self-transcendence and conservation values and an increase in self-enhancement [R7, abstract]. This is a real cohort or period shift, but period and cohort are still entangled across two time points.
- **Very large applicant series.** 82,147 aviation applicants aged 17–24, born 1965–2002 and tested between 1987 and 2019 [R8, PDF p1]: "The generational differences found exhibited extremely small effect sizes" [R8, PDF p1]. The authors concluded that generational differences in personality "do not significantly impact training and safety considerations" [R8, PDF p8].
- **Replicated cross-sections of collective memory** (1985, 2000 and after 2001) examine whether memories of events formed in adolescence and early adulthood remain stable over time [R9, abstract]. This is the mechanism a cohort explanation would need, studied outside work.

The better the design, the smaller and more specific the differences. This is the core caution for any knowledge-exchange study built on generation labels.

### 3. Generations are not homogeneous

A three-sample study set out to "demonstrate that there are differences within the Millennial generation that affect work values, preferences for work/life balance, and attraction to employer attributes" [R10, PDF p1]. It found these differences by age, gender, relationship status and nationality, concluding that "Millennials are not as homogeneous as we assumed" [R10, PDF p1]. Nationality, for instance, affected 13 of 19 employer attributes [R10, PDF p12].

### 4. Knowledge exchange itself is studied through mechanisms, not labels

The studies that address transmission directly do not rely on cohort labels:

- A grandparent–parent–grandchild study (187 triads) found that "role modeling mediated the relationships between grandparents', parents', and grandchildren's career adapt- ability" [R11, PDF p1]. Some direct links were non-significant [R11, PDF p5]. Transmission ran through an observable behaviour (role modeling), not through generation membership.
- An organizational case study of intergenerational knowledge transfer identified a source–recipient model and a mutual-exchange model. Its conclusion was that a supportive context allowed both explicit and tacit knowledge to be transferred [R12, abstract].
- A conceptual framework for Generation Y development proposes mentoring and knowledge-sharing routes [R13, abstract]. It is untested.

## Conclusions this collection supports

1. **Generation labels do not explain knowledge exchange in this literature.** Where designs can separate cohort from age [R7, R8], differences are small or domain-specific. Single cross-sections [R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6] cannot attribute differences to generation at all.
2. **Within-generation variation is large** [R10], which undermines policies aimed at a "generation".
3. **Researchable mechanisms exist**: role modeling [R11], source–recipient vs. mutual exchange structures [R12] and mentoring [R13]. A study of knowledge exchange across career stages should measure career stage, tenure and age directly and test these mechanisms, with generation at most a descriptive marker.

## Limits

- 15 included studies from one curated folder, with only one case study of workplace knowledge transfer [R12]. The knowledge-exchange evidence itself is thin.
- Machine-coded design labels in the evidence table are screening aids; the design classifications in the text are hand-coded from abstracts and the cited pages.

## Proposed research direction

The companion protocol proposes dyadic mentor–mentee or senior–junior pairs measured over time. It records each person's age, career stage and tenure separately, and measures knowledge-exchange behaviours (help seeking, advice giving, reverse mentoring) and role modeling. Generation is used only descriptively. The design remains a proposal pending population, access and ethics decisions.

# Paper 15 — Empirical protocol v2: Knowledge exchange across career stages, not generations

> **Status: PROPOSAL awaiting AMET University Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) approval.** No data have been collected; no results exist. Sample sizes are computed from **assumed** smallest effects of interest, not from any study. Instruments are ScaleScope catalogue entries whose source articles were resolved on Crossref (9 October 2026). Version 2 replaces the v1 draft `paper-15-oct-2024-protocol.md`.

## 1. Research question
Do career stage and tenure, rather than generation labels, predict knowledge exchange in senior-junior pairs, and is role modelling the mechanism?

## 2. Hypotheses (to be pre-registered)
- H1: Tenure and career stage predict knowledge sharing beyond age.
- H2: Role modelling mediates the senior-to-junior effect on junior knowledge sharing.
- H3: Generation categories add no explained variance once age, tenure and career stage are entered.

## 3. Design
Dyadic two-wave study of senior-junior pairs.

**Measurement occasions**
- T1: both members
- T2 (3 months): both members

## 4. Population, eligibility and recruitment
**Population(s):** AMET University faculty and administrative staff; working professionals in India (organisations reached through alumni, professional networks and recruiter contacts).

**Eligibility:** Pairs with a mentoring or regular work relationship for 3+ months. Exclusion: failing two or more embedded attention checks; incomplete primary measures at the analysed wave (handled under §8).

**Recruitment and independence safeguards**
- **AMET faculty and staff** — invitation sent by the study team through an institution-wide mailing list with Registrar permission, **not through line managers or HoDs**; nothing is reported at a level smaller than 5 respondents; no participation data reach appraisers.
- **Working professionals in India** — via alumni networks, professional associations and LinkedIn posts; where organisational data (HR records, supervisor ratings) are needed, a signed **organisational access letter / data-sharing agreement** is obtained first and the organisation never sees individual responses.

## 5. Measures
| Construct | Instrument (ScaleScope id) | Items | Occasion | Source article (Crossref-verified) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Knowledge sharing | Knowledge Sharing Scale (KSS, #14) | 10 | T1, T2 | [10.1108/13673270410567675](https://doi.org/10.1108/13673270410567675) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |
| Career stage, tenure, age | Records / study-specific items (no published instrument needed) | — | T1 study-specific demographic items (age in years, organisational and occupational tenure, self-placed career stage) | — | define and pilot; record access needs consent and a data agreement where organisational |
| Role modelling | Mentoring Functions Questionnaire — role-modelling factor (outside catalogue) | see source (15 items, 3 factors) | T1, T2, junior member; role-modelling factor of the Mentoring Functions Questionnaire | [10.1006/jvbe.1993.1046](https://doi.org/10.1006/jvbe.1993.1046) | confirm permission/licence; measure and item count confirmed in an open paper using it (see instrument file); check wording against the original |

All instruments are administered in English (the working language of the target population). Any translation or wording adaptation (e.g. day-level or target-shifted versions) is labelled **adapted — not validated**, piloted with cognitive interviews (n ≈ 10) and checked for factor structure before the main study.

## 6. Sample size
Monte Carlo simulation (1,000 replications per N; joint-significance test, standardized a = b = 0.26) gives **160** for 80% power (simulation code `power.py::n_indirect_joint`; a = b = .39 → 72 and .20 → 270 as checks). With assumed attrition/exclusion of 25% across waves, recruit **214**. *Assumption:* Dyad-level indirect effect, standardized paths .26 assumed (simulation).

Target completers: **160**; recruitment target: **214**. Power will be re-checked by simulation with pilot variances before pre-registration; if the target is not reachable, the study is reported as estimation (confidence intervals) rather than as a confirmatory test.

## 7. Procedure and timing
1. IEC approval → OSF pre-registration (hypotheses, analysis, exclusions, stopping rule) → pilot (n ≈ 30, not analysed for hypotheses).
2. Recruitment window ≈ 6 weeks per wave; two reminders per wave; reminders stop on withdrawal.
3. Waves linked by a self-generated pseudonymous code; the linking key is stored separately from responses.
4. Data collection ends when the recruitment target is met or the pre-registered end date passes, whichever is first.

## 8. Analysis plan
Actor-partner interdependence models; indirect effect by Monte Carlo CI.

- **Missing data:** full-information maximum likelihood (or multiple imputation, 20+ imputations) under MAR; attrition analysed against baseline variables and reported.
- **Measurement:** CFA for each multi-item measure; reliability (ω and α) reported; measurement invariance across waves/groups before comparing means or paths.
- **Inference:** two-sided α = .05; effect sizes with 95% CIs; Holm correction across the confirmatory hypothesis family; exploratory analyses labelled as such.
- **Common-method bias:** temporal separation and, where planned, other-source ratings; a marker variable is included in the survey.

## 9. Ethics (ICMR 2017 National Ethical Guidelines)
- **Risk category:** Minimal risk — request **expedited review**. Rationale: Questions about everyday work experiences; no deception, no intervention, no identifiable data published.
- **Consent:** written/electronic informed consent before any question; separate consent items for each optional element (record linkage, co-worker/supervisor contact, follow-up waves).
- **Voluntariness:** no penalty for non-participation or withdrawal; no data from or to supervisors/appraisers at individual level.
- **Confidentiality & data protection:** pseudonymised data, linking key held only by the PI on an encrypted drive; processing consistent with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; retention 5 years after publication (or as the IEC directs), then deletion.
- **Support:** debrief page with the national tele-mental-health helpline (Tele-MANAS, 14416 — verify before use) and contact details of the PI and IEC.
- Ethics pack (IEC application summary, participant information sheet, consent form, debrief): `../ethics/paper-15-oct-2024-ethics-pack.md`.

## 10. Open science
OSF pre-registration before data collection; de-identified data and analysis code shared on OSF after publication where consent permits (HR-record and organisational data excluded unless the organisation agrees).

## 11. Approvals and readiness checklist
- [ ] Instrument items obtained

- [ ] Panel provider selected and costed (if panel used)

- [ ] OSF pre-registration (link: ________)

## B. Participant information sheet
**Study:** Knowledge exchange across career stages, not generations

**Why are we doing this study?** Our research question is: Do career stage and tenure, rather than generation labels, predict knowledge exchange in senior-junior pairs, and is role modelling the mechanism?

**What will I be asked to do?** Complete online questionnaires (about 15–20 minutes per survey) on 2 occasion(s) as described: T1: both members; T2 (3 months): both members.

**Do I have to take part?** No. Taking part is voluntary. You can stop at any time and withdraw your answers up to the point the data are anonymised for analysis [date], without giving a reason and without any effect on your job, appraisal or relationship with your organisation.

**Risks:** We do not expect any risk beyond everyday life. You can skip any question.

**Benefits:** No direct benefit; a summary of findings will be offered.

**Confidentiality:** Your answers are linked across surveys by a code you create, not by your name. Your supervisor or organisation will never see your individual answers. Results are reported only for groups of 5 or more.

**Contacts:** PI [name, e-mail, phone]; AMET University IEC Member Secretary [name, e-mail, phone]. Support: Tele-MANAS national helpline 14416 (verify before use).
